::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: In iris, the association between sepal length and width differs between setosa and virginica (r = 0.743 vs 0.457), and complete data detect the difference at p = .025.

table.header: 5. Applied illustration: a real species difference made to disappear
table.expanded: In base-R iris, sepal length and sepal width are positively associated within each species, and the strength differs: r = 0.743 in setosa and 0.457 in virginica (N = 100, 50 per species), so the complete-data Fisher-z contrast is ζ_full = z(0.743) -z(0.457) = 0.4623, SE 0.2063, z = 2.24, p = 0.025almost exactly the simulated design value, and significant.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 895 columns across 78 data files.
#### Issues Identified
4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("p36imp_osf_bundle_20261007_v5.zip/osf_bundle/results/variants_b3_0.0_MAR.csv", "p36imp_osf_bundle_20261007_v5.zip/osf_bundle/results/variants_b3_0.0_MCAR.csv", "p36imp_osf_bundle_paper1_2026-10-27_2044_56f9ba37.zip/osf_bundle/results/variants_b3_0.0_MAR.csv", "p36imp_osf_bundle_paper1_2026-10-27_2044_56f9ba37.zip/osf_bundle/results/variants_b3_0.0_MCAR.csv" ), Column = c("rel_bias", "rel_bias", "rel_bias", "rel_bias"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 48 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 48 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 48 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 48 values are missing" )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 78 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

**`os.chdir()` in the code**
**1 script calls `os.chdir()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with `pass`. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring an `os.chdir()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

Missing data are ordinary, and the standard advice for handling them is to use multiple imputation.
That advice is sound and it is also underspecified: "multiple imputation" names a family of procedures, and which member you get depends on choices that software makes for you.
This paper is about one such choice, in a setting where it decides the answer.
The setting is a comparison of associations across groups.

A researcher asks whether two variables are more strongly related in one group than another -whether the link between sleep and mood is tighter in adolescents than in adults, whether a biomarker tracks outcome more closely in treated than untreated patients.
The estimand is a difference of correlations, which we take on the Fisher-z scale, ζ = z(ρ₁) -z(ρ₂), z(r) = artanh(r).
One of the two variables is incomplete.
The analyst imputes it and proceeds.
A plain correlation cannot exhibit the failure we study, and that fact determines the design.
If (X, Y) is bivariate normal and X is missing-at-random (MAR) on Y, then imputing X from Y by linear regression is the correct conditional distribution.
The naive and the principled imputation model coincide; there is no uncongeniality to find.
A partial correlation in a jointly normal world is safe for the same reason.
A reader who has met the congeniality literature (Meng, 1994) and expects trouble from any correlation estimand will not find it in this one.

text.text: The trouble appears when the analysis is group-heterogeneous while the imputation pools.
The analyst's model grants each group its own association.
The default imputation model grants each group its own mean and forces a common slope.
That omitted group × Y interaction is the precise analogue of the omitted product term that damages interaction estimates, and it is the object of this paper.
That default is not a hypothetical workflow.

Main-effects-only imputation is what three widely used programs do unless told otherwise: SPSS imputes with INTERACTIONS=NONE; mice adds no interaction terms unless the user constructs them; Stata requires an explicit include() or by().

Defaults vary by program, procedure, variable type and the formulas a user supplies, so we describe this as a common main-effects-only default workflow rather than as the behaviour of imputation software in general.
An analyst who accepts these defaults, having done nothing wrong by the letter of the standard advice, is running the arm we show fails.
The difference is attenuated by a factor we can write down.
The completed within-group covariance is a blend: the observed cases carry the group's own association, the imputed cases carry the pooled slope.
The pooled slope is common to both groups, so it cancels in the difference, and what survives is shrunk to the observed-case share.
The result is ζ → (1κ(π))•ζ with κ derived in closed form, verified step by step against simulation, and evaluable by quadrature for any missingness rate.
Coverage gets worse as the sample grows.
The bias is a fixed fraction of the estimand while the standard error shrinks at rate 1/√N, so the ratio of the two grows without bound.
Nominal 95% coverage falls from 0.992 at N = 40 to 0.703 at N = 320 with 40% missing.
This inverts the intuition researchers actually use: it is the larger, better-powered study that is most confidently wrong, and nothing in its output signals it.
At small N the pooled arm's intervals are conservative -0.992 coverage looks reassuring -so the failure arrives precisely when the study is finally big enough to be believed.
The failure has an exact boundary, and we can state it.

When the groups share both a common X | Y slope and a common residual variance, pooled imputation moves nothing: each group's correlation comes back at its true value, and so does any contrast between them, for any selection on Y, however asymmetric, and at every missing rate.
Inside that class pooling neither shrinks a real difference nor invents one.
The attenuation this paper is about therefore happens outside it -in the standardised design a real correlation difference is a slope difference, which is what pooling moves.

The practical consequence is still asymmetric, because in that design a true null satisfies the condition while a real difference violates it: a reported difference has not been produced by the imputation, and an absent one is uninformative.

The condition is sufficient, and necessary in the rate, but it is one on population quantities rather than on anything a reader can read off a published table; §Discussion gives the reanalysis rule that follows.
That condition is not "equal correlations", which is what the standardised design makes it look like.
Nor is it equal slopes alone: the slope governs the completed covariance, but the residual variance governs the completed variance of the imputed variable, and a correlation needs both.

Holding the slope fixed at 0.400 in both groups while letting the residual variance differ four-fold still yields a plim of ζ = -0.119 -a probability limit, what ζ converges to as N grows -under a true null (results/sequel_boundary_two_conditions.csv).
The slope is β_g = ρ_g•σ_Xg/σ_Yg, so two groups with the same correlation but different variances have different slopes -and then pooled imputation manufactures a difference.
With ρ₁ = ρ₂ = 0.40 and a two-fold ratio in the spread of the complete variable, the plim of ζ is -0.121, as large as the attenuation of a real difference at 20% missing (-0.123, §Results 1).
Since groups compared in practice routinely differ in variance, the usable rule includes that check.
It happens on real data.
In iris, the association between sepal length and width differs between setosa and virginica (r = 0.743 vs 0.457), and complete data detect the difference at p = .025.
With 40% of sepal-width values missing at random, the default imputation model detects it in none of 2000 replications.
Group-wise imputation detects it as often as listwise deletion does.

That dataset also transports the theory to a design it was not derived for: it is unbalanced and not exactly normal, its two species lose very different fractions of data, and the closed form still predicts the incremental damage of pooling to within 0.010.
It is one worked application, repeatedly masked, not replication across datasets.
That imputation models omitting a needed term bias the corresponding estimate is established, and we do not rediscover it.

Omitting an interaction from the imputation model attenuates that interaction (von Hippel, 2009; Seaman, Bartlett & White, 2012); substantive-model-compatible imputation repairs it (Bartlett, Seaman, White & Carpenter, 2015); and imputing within groups -our group-wise arm -goes back to von Hippel (2009), who named it stratify, then impute and whom Enders and Gottschall (2011) credit.

text.text: §Related work sets out what each established.

We add three things: a magnitude for a correlation-difference estimand, in closed form rather than tabulated; the direction of the failure in N, which changes how a reader should read a large study; and a proof of a sufficient invariance boundary, which converts the finding into an asymmetric reading rule rather than a general warning.
The premise is not ours: Enders (2022, §10.2) states that a correlation differing by group implies a two-way interaction, and recommends imputing each group separately.
Enders does not state the cost of ignoring it.

We are not aware of a prior small-sample study comparing pooled against group-wise imputation for a between-group correlation difference, or of an analytic bias expression for this estimand -a statement about our searches, which we describe, not a claim that none exists.

The closest neighbour is Tilling et al. (2016): their stratified imputation is our group-wise arm under another name, and they report the same ultra-conservatism under a true null that we find one estimand over.

text.text: An analysis that lets two groups differ in association, filled from an imputation model that grants each group its own mean but a common slope, is uncongenial to it in a specific and diagnosable way, since the omitted term is the group × Y interaction.
Everything below is a variation on that single mechanism, differing only in which estimand carries it.

text.text: Three of their findings touch this paper directly, and on two of them they have priority.
The first is that their stratified imputation is our group-wise arm.
Where one variable in the interaction is fully observed and categorical, they split the data by it and impute within strata, which makes the omitted interaction unnecessary.
That is exactly the remedy we recommend, arrived at independently and credited here.

They also identify its boundary: stratification fails when the stratifying variable is continuous and split at its mean, because "within each half of the data set, there is still an association between Y and the interaction term XZ which is not being taken account of."
Our grouping variable is categorical, so our arm is not exposed to that failure -but the boundary is theirs.
The second is that they report overcoverage under a true null, which we did not know when we derived it.

Their summary of what is new includes the result, the last of its four bullets: when the interaction is truly zero and the imputation model omits it, confidence intervals overcover, reaching roughly 99% against a nominal 95% and rising at larger samples.
Their explanation is the one we give, that "the analyst is 'assuming' less than the imputer," which they attribute to Meng (1994) in their Discussion.
text.formatted: Their explanation is the one we give, that "the analyst is 'assuming' less than the imputer," which they attribute to <ref type="bibr">Meng (1994)</ref> in their Discussion.

text.text: This is the ultra-conservatism we report under the null in §Results 4, one estimand over.
We found it independently, but we did not find it first.
The third is that they report coverage worsening with sample size, in passing.
Comparing n = 2,000 with n = 20,000, they note that "coverage of the MI without interactions is lower" at the larger sample.
That observation occupies a single clause, its numbers sit in supplementary tables, and their own summary box does not mention it.
It is nonetheless reported, so any claim that the direction is undocumented would be false.

Paper 1 of this series, More Data, Worse Inference (Shavit, 2026a), treats the same mechanism for a continuous × continuous interaction coefficient: there the imputation model omits the product term rather than the group × Y term, and the attenuation follows a factor of the same form.
We refer to it below where the two results differ.
Against that table, four things are not in it.
The first is a magnitude, in closed form.
Every study above establishes that an omitted interaction biases the corresponding estimate, but none reports the size.
We give ζ → (1κ(π))•ζ with κ evaluable by quadrature for any missingness rate, and a general form covering unequal group sizes, means, variances and selection rates.
The second is the correlation-difference estimand itself.
The literature above concerns regression coefficients and product terms, whereas a difference of correlations is a rescaled slope difference.

That rescaling is what makes the failure two-directional, because the completed covariance and the completed variance are damaged through different channels, which in turn is why the boundary requires two conditions rather than one.
The third is the direction in N, given as a curve.

Tilling et al. have the observation at two very large sample sizes for binary covariates, whereas we trace it across N = 40-320 with Monte Carlo standard errors, for continuous variables, together with the bias and standard-error decomposition that explains the direction rather than merely exhibiting it.
The fourth is the manufactured difference, and here prior work narrows what we may claim.

Yamaguchi, Ueno, Maruo and Gosho (2020) report that when treatment groups in a longitudinal trial are heteroscedastic, imputing them from a single pooled model biases the treatment-effect estimate and degrades coverage, and that imputing separately by group repairs it.
That is our mechanism, in which unequal group scale breaks a pooled imputation model, applied to a difference in means rather than in correlations.
We did not find it before deriving the correlation case, and it constrains what we may claim.
Our remaining claim is narrower and, we think, still worth reporting.
Theirs is bias in a non-null effect, whereas ours is a false positive from a true null, in which ρ₁ = ρ₂ exactly and the procedure invents a difference.

Theirs is simulation across variance structures, whereas ours is a closed form that predicts the size of the spurious effect and states the exact condition under which it vanishes, namely that the groups share a slope and, unless that shared slope is zero, a residual variance.
We also report the Type I error rising with sample size, from 0.03 at N = 80 to 0.31 at N = 640, which is the operational consequence and which we did not find reported anywhere.

Tilling et al.'s null-case result runs the other way, theirs being overcoverage where ours is a false positive, because binary covariates entering a common model do not carry separate scales and their design therefore cannot violate the condition that ours violates.
We should be plain about what "closed form" does and does not distinguish us.

Analytic bias expressions for multiple imputation are an established genre: Curnow et al. (2023) derive a maximum-bias expression for a regression coefficient when a collider is admitted to the imputation model as an auxiliary variable, and use it on real cohort data to bound the damage.

The new element is the estimand, not the expression: a difference of correlations rather than a single coefficient, and a wholly manufactured effect from a true null rather than distortion of a real one.
Curnow et al. note in their Discussion that an exposure-confounder interaction would make their expression more complicated, and do not derive it.
Our group-wise arm is not new; saying precisely what is old delimits what we add.

Enders and Gottschall (2011) call it separate group imputation -it "imputes the data separately for each of the G subgroups," crediting von Hippel (2009) for stratify, then impute -and find it beats product term imputation, which admits group through code and product variables.
Their diagnosis is the one we formalise: product term imputation "implicitly uses a homoscedastic model," and fails when group variances differ.

Note their pooled comparator is better specified than ours, which enters group as a main effect only; that a model with the product terms still fails is stronger evidence for the mechanism than our own comparison supplies.

Their bias, though, attenuates group differences toward the mean, raising Type II error, where our second result is a false positive from a true null -so they credit our attenuation and leave the manufactured difference untouched, as Tilling et al.'s null-case overcoverage does.
They also answer, in advance, the objection this design invites.

Enders and Gottschall note that their simulations were in one sense "rigged" against product term imputation, because the models always implied group differences in the population variances, and then report how large those differences were: F-max values, the ratio of the largest group variance to the smallest, spanning 1.10 to 2.00 across their three simulation models -differences "many researchers would consider … to be relatively small and well within the range of differences that would routinely appear in applied research."
Failing to preserve differences that small, they find, "can lead to substantial bias."
Our design is more austere than theirs.
Both variables are standard normal in both groups, so the F-max on either manifest variable is exactly 1, and an analyst who compared group variances would see nothing at all.

The heteroscedasticity is confined to the imputation residual, Var(X | Y) = 1 -ρ²_g, which is 0.64 in the first group against 0.96 in the second: a ratio of 1.5, sitting inside the range they call routine.
The pooled model does not need visible heteroscedasticity to fail.
It needs only the kind that a table of group variances cannot show.
By 2022 it is textbook.
Enders (2022, §10.2) recommends group-wise imputation for our exact situation -correlations by gender -on our exact premise: "a correlation that differs by gender implies a two-way interaction."
We are therefore not proposing the remedy; we are pricing the failure.

He compares group-wise against model-based imputation, both congenial, and reports they agree; the pooled, main-effectsonly model that software gives by default is not among the arms he compares there, so that section reports no bias, coverage or rejection rate for it.
Ours remains the closed form, the estimand, the behaviour in N, and the boundary.
The interaction case has been examined by simulation.

Smith et al. (2025) compare passive imputation, just-another-variable, stratify-impute-append and substantive-model-compatible imputation for a logistic model containing an interaction, and find the last two least biased.

Their stratify-impute-append arm is the nearest published relative of our group-wise imputation; their setting is logistic rather than linear, their sample size is fixed at 10,000, and they report no analytic expression.
They also bound how far that remedy carries: stratify-impute-append performed poorly in their study when the fully observed variable in the interaction had a continuous underlying form.
Our stratifying variable is a categorical group, so the boundary does not apply here, but it is their result and it belongs in this paragraph.
All of this is a statement about the searches we have run, which the Method describes, not a claim that no other such report exists.

We ask how the choice of imputation model governs recovery of a between-group difference in correlation when one of the two correlated variables is incomplete, and we characterise the resulting bias analytically rather than only empirically.
Two questions organise the study: 1.

When the imputation model pools an association across groups -a common main-effects-only default, which enters group as a main effect -by how much is the between-group difference attenuated, and does that attenuation follow a law?
As the sample grows, what happens to confidence-interval coverage?
The study follows ADEMP (Morris, White & Crowther, 2019) and reports Monte Carlo standard errors on every performance measure.

§Introduction gives the reason: when (X, Y) is bivariate normal, regressing X on Y is the correct conditional distribution, so the naive and the congenial imputation models coincide and no uncongeniality can arise -for a plain correlation and for a partial correlation alike.
The split becomes real as soon as the analysis is group-heterogeneous while the imputation pools.
The analyst's model allows each group its own association; the imputation model allows each group its own mean but forces a common X | Y slope.
The omitted group × Y interaction in the imputation model is the exact analogue of the omitted product term in the companion paper, and it is what makes the imputation uncongenial to the analysis.
Two equal-sized groups, g ∈ {1, 2}, with N/2 observations each.
Within group g, (X, Y) ~BVN(0, 0, 1, 1, ρ_g), so both variables are marginally standard normal in both groups and the groups differ only in the strength of association.
The estimand is the difference on the Fisher-z scale,

X is missing at random, with missingness depending on the fully observed Y: logit P(X missing | Y) = γ₀ + 0.7•Y, with γ₀ calibrated by root-finding so that the marginal missing fraction equals π ∈ {0.20, 0.40}.

Because Y is standard normal in both groups, the two groups lose the same expected fraction -a deliberate simplification whose asymmetric counterpart appears in the applied illustration, where it matters.
Selection on Y alone is not an incidental choice.

It is what preserves E[X | Y, observed] = ρ_g•Y, so the observed cases still carry each group's own association and the entire distortion is attributable to the imputation model rather than to selection on X.

The range is chosen to straddle the sample sizes at which a correlation-difference test is actually run in applied work, and to make the behaviour in N visible rather than reporting a single N.

It is not a straw man: main-effects-only imputation is a genuine default in three programs applied researchers use -SPSS imputes with INTERACTIONS=NONE, mice adds no interaction terms unless the user builds them, and Stata requires an explicit include() or by() to do otherwise.
Defaults differ across programs, procedures and variable types, so the claim is about this common workflow rather than about imputation software as a class.
An analyst who accepts these defaults gets the MI-pooled arm.
Imputations are proper: each draw takes (β, σ) from the posterior of the Bayesian normal linear regression and then draws imputed values with residual noise.

Those draws carry the uncertainty the imputation model implies, which is a weaker property than calibrated inference about the correlation contrast, and the two come apart when the imputation model and the analysis disagree.

§Results 4 measures the gap at the one design where pooling gets the point estimate exactly right: the pooled arm's estimates still carry roughly half the congenial arm's sampling variability, and the pooled arm rejects a true null 3 times in 1000 against a nominal 50.
So the point estimate is not the only thing this arm can get wrong.
Within each group, r_g is the Pearson correlation of the completed data, and the estimate is ζ = z(r1)z(r2) with the Fisher-z Wald standard error SE = √( 1/(n₁ -3) + 1/(n₂ -3) ).
Multiple-imputation estimates are combined by Rubin's rules on the Fisher-z scale, back-transforming only for reporting, with the small-sample degrees of freedom of Barnard and Rubin (1999).
This is the standard procedure rather than our construction.

Enders (2022, p. 406) states it in three steps -transform each of the M correlations, average, back-transform -because "the sampling distribution of r becomes increasingly skewed as the population correlation moves away from zero"; White, Royston and Wood (2011, Table VIII) list the correlation among the statistics needing a transformation before Rubin's rules apply; and van Buuren (2018, §5.2.2) gives the z-scale variance 1/(n -3).

text.text: One caveat we state rather than bury: Barnard-Rubin has not been specifically validated for this estimand.
We use it as the conservative choice.
It widens intervals, so it cannot manufacture the coverage collapse we report; if anything it understates it.

For each cell: bias on the z scale, empirical SE, RMSE, empirical 95% coverage, and rejection rate (power under the alternative designs, Type I error under the null), each with its Monte Carlo standard error.
We also report the empirical attenuation the fraction of the true difference that the method removes, which is the quantity the closed form predicts.
To carry the result onto data readers recognise, we repeat the design on iris, comparing setosa and virginica on the association between sepal length and sepal width.
The complete-data contrast is treated as the truth an analyst would have reported; MAR missingness is imposed on sepal width 2000 times and each method re-estimates.

The pooled arm's bias is flat in N. It is not a small-sample artefact that more data will cure: eight times the sample changes the bias at π = 0.40 from -0.242 to -0.228, a shift of 0.014 against a combined Monte Carlo standard error of 0.0085 -1.7 standard errors, consistent with no change.
Group-wise imputation is unbiased throughout.
Listwise deletion loses efficiency -empirical SE 0.142 against 0.083 for pooled at N = 320, π = 0.40 -and it carries a small bias of its own, which the Listwise column above shows.

Selection on Y shrinks the observed-case variance of Y from 1 to v_o = 0.907 at 40% missing, so each group's complete-case correlation is range-restricted to ρ_g√v_o ⁄ √(ρ_g²•v_o + 1 -ρ_g²): 0.581 and 0.191 against 0.6 and 0.2.

The gap that opens, z(r_cc) -z(ρ_g), falls strictly as ρ_g rises -from -0.010 at ρ = 0.2 to -0.029 at ρ = 0.6 -so where both groups face the same selection the two attenuations cancel in the difference if and only if the two correlations are equal.
That is the null case of §4, not this design.

The probability limit here is -0.0194 on the z scale at π = 0.40 and -0.0132 at π = 0.20, a κ_listwise of 0.040 against the pooled arm's 0.457 -under a tenth of the damage, and 3.2 to 4.2 Monte Carlo standard errors from zero in three of the four Listwise cells at N ≥ 160 (verify/p36_h1_listwise_rangerestriction_2026-10-07.py).
Figure 1 shows why, before any of the arithmetic.

text.text: Panel A is the complete data, with two genuinely different slopes.

In panel B a single pooled imputation model supplies every missing value from one common slope, so the stronger association is pulled down and the weaker one pulled up; the gap closes from 0.48 to 0.34 in the draw shown.
Panel C lets each group keep its own imputation model and the gap survives at 0.49.
The difference the analyst measures in panel B is a difference between slopes the imputation has already partly equalised.
(The panels show one realisation, so the pooled value sits near rather than on the closed-form plim of 0.27 quoted beneath them.)
The mechanism is arithmetic rather than subtle -the bias is fixed while the interval narrows at rate 1/√N, so the ratio of bias to standard error grows without bound.

That inversion is the point: more data makes the inference worse, and nothing signals it, because the pooled arm's intervals are if anything wider than nominal at small N (0.992 coverage at N = 40 looks reassuring).
The robustness design reproduces it and then some: coverage 0.984 → 0.584 (π = 0.40, N = 40 → 320), and 0.989 → 0.862 at π = 0.20.
The same distortion costs detections.

At π = 0.40, N = 320 the pooled arm rejects ζ = 0 in 0.482 of replications against group-wise imputation's 0.897 -the default imputation model halves the power to find a real difference (results/sequel_grid.csv, power).
Sources: §Theory; R/verify_conj011.
R; R/drv004_closedform.R; results/sequel_kappa_curve_cf.csv.
The identification b = (ρ₁ + ρ₂)/2 is exact under this design and not in general.

It holds because the groups are equal-sized, Y is standard normal in both, and the missingness rule is therefore symmetric across them, so the pooled fit weights the two groups equally: verified numerically at N = 4 × 10⁵, where the pooled slope is 0.4011 on complete data and 0.4032 on the MAR-observed cases against a nominal 0.400.

Where selection is asymmetric -as in the applied illustration, and as in most real data -the pooled slope is neither (ρ₁ + ρ₂)/2 nor equal to its complete-data value, and it must be computed rather than assumed. §5a handles that case by evaluating the procedure directly rather than by substituting into this expression.
The reading is the whole paper in one line.
The observed cases carry the group's own association; the imputed cases carry the pooled slope.
The pooled slope is by construction common to both groups, so it cancels in the difference -and what survives is the group-specific part, shrunk to the observed-case share A ≈ 1π.
The closed form and κ columns are quadrature, read from results/sequel_kappa_curve_cf.csv; the simulation column is Monte Carlo and is labelled as such.
At R = 1000 the grid recovers κ = 0.2515 (π = .20, Monte Carlo SE 0.0065) and 0.4641 (π = .40, SE 0.0053) against the predicted 0.2512 and 0.4567.

The first sits 0.05 Monte Carlo standard errors from its prediction and the second 1.4, so the two agree within simulation error rather than to three decimals -a distinction worth keeping, because the π = .40 pair differs in the second decimal.
The robustness pair gives 0.2477 and 0.4599 against 0.2509 and 0.4571, reproducing the near-invariance to the ρ pair at full replication.
Source: results/sequel_kappa_curve_cf.csv (closed form), results/sequel_kappa_curve_sim.csv (anchors, R = 500), figure results/sequel_kappa_curve.png.
Two points cannot show a law, so we evaluate the closed form on a fine grid of π and simulate anchors at π ∈ {.10, .20, .30, .40, .50} × N ∈ {160, 320}.

Figure 3 plots the two together: the curve is the closed form, the points are simulation, and the claim that κ is a law rather than a summary of two cells rests on the points lying on the curve across the whole range.

text.text: The closed form is evaluated by quadrature, not by Monte Carlo; the Appendix explains why simulation is not accurate enough for this comparison.
Agreement is within 0.015 across the whole range and within 0.005 for π ≥ 0.30.

The one systematic departure is at π = 0.10, where κ sits about 0.015 below the predicted value at both sample sizes -roughly 1.7 Monte Carlo SEs, and worth stating rather than smoothing: at low missingness the finite-sample estimate of a small attenuation is itself slightly attenuated.
The two pairs sharing a gap of 0.40 at different levels agree to within 0.001 across the entire π range -0.4567 against 0.4571 at π = 0.40.

That is numerical near-invariance over the levels we evaluated, not a proved invariance: we have no derivation showing that κ is exactly free of the level, and the Fisher transform and the completed variances give no reason to expect one.
But κ rises with the gap between the correlations, gently up to a gap of about 0.4 and steeply beyond.

The honest statement is that κ depends on the full design, κ = κ(π, ρ₁, ρ₂) -the two pairs sharing a gap of 0.40 still disagree by 0.0004, so the gap is not an exact second argument, only a near-invariant summary of the level dependence over the pairs we tested.
For applied purposes little changes: across the range of differences researchers usually test (gap ≤ 0.4) κ varies by under 0.01 and may be read off the curve as a function of π alone.
κ exceeds π everywhere, and most where data are nearly complete.
The ratio κ/π declines monotonically from 1.40 at π = 0.05 to 1.07 at π = 0.60.
The super-proportionality is therefore strongest exactly at the missingness rates applied researchers meet -at 10% missing data the difference is attenuated by 13%, not 10%.
This is a property of this MAR-on-Y selection: the steepening comes from selection concentrating the observed cases where Y is informative, and a different mechanism would give a different curve.
It is not a universal constant of pooled imputation.
Coverage degrades smoothly in π as well as in N. At N = 320 the pooled arm's 95% coverage runs 0.960, 0.898, 0.796, 0.688, 0.528 across π = .10 … .50 (MCSEs 0.009-0.022).
This sweep is the R = 500 anchor run; §2's headline 0.703 at π = .40 is the R = 1000 grid, so the two numbers for that one cell are two replications of it and not a disagreement about it.
Group-wise imputation over the same twenty cells holds bias in [-0.016, +0.021] and coverage in [0.936, 0.974].
Sources: §Theory; results/sequel_spurious_twin.csv.
We hypothesised a mirror image of the companion paper's spurious-interaction result: that group-asymmetric missingness would make pooled imputation invent a correlation difference where none exists.
It does not, and the closed form explains why.

Two qualifications, both established below.

The identity is design-specific in its value but not its structure: Under the null, pooled imputation is not anti-conservative but ultra-conservative -its estimates have roughly half the sampling variability of the congenial arm, because pulling both groups toward a common slope suppresses the very variability the test needs.

A test that rejects a true null 3 times in 1000 against a nominal 50 is not a well-behaved test; it is miscalibrated in the other direction, and the attenuated point estimate, the halved power of §2 and this near-zero Type I rate are three faces of one invalid procedure rather than three separate findings.
Nothing below should be read as reassurance about the procedure.
Where the groups share both a slope and a residual variance, pooling returns each correlation at its true value, so it shrinks nothing and invents nothing.

The standardised design, not that class, makes the reading rule asymmetric: there a true null sits inside the class, while a real difference means unequal slopes and so falls outside it and is shrunk.
A pooled-imputation analysis that finds a group difference has therefore not manufactured it, but one that finds none may well have erased it.

Equal correlations with unequal group variances means unequal slopes, and then pooled imputation manufactures a difference from nothing - §4b reports a rejection rate of 0.309 at N = 640 against a nominal 0.05.
The unconditional reading of the heading above is false, and it is the more quotable version, so we disarm it where a reader meets it.
Source: R/sequel_mnar_boundary.R; results/sequel_mnar_plim.csv, results/sequel_mnar_type1.csv.
The proof above uses two things: the identity A_g + B_g = 1, which holds for any selection on Y, and
The first is easy to remember and the second easy to drop, and the result is then restated as holding for any selection mechanism whatsoever.
It does not, and the difference is worth establishing rather than hedging.
Under the null (ρ₁ = ρ₂ = 0.40, π = 0.40), evaluated at N = 2 × 10⁶, with every mechanism calibrated to the same rate in each group so that a rate difference cannot drive the result.
Each arm is judged against its own Monte Carlo standard error, because the three arms do not share one.
Listwise deletion sees only the roughly 6.0 × 10⁵ cases per group that survived deletion, so its standard error is √[1/(n₁ -3) + 1/(n₂ -3)] = 0.00183.
Both imputed arms carry all 10⁶ cases per group, and for the pooled arm the nominal complete-data value 0.00141 is the right yardstick.
For group-wise imputation it is not: a single proper draw filling 40% of X adds noise the nominal figure does not count, and the realised standard error is 0.00218, 1.54 times nominal.

Dividing the whole table by one 0.00141 -which is what an earlier version of this section did -therefore overstates every listwise multiple by 29% and every group-wise multiple by 54%, and the error is largest exactly where the section's conclusion lives.

Measured directly at this N over 200 replications of the MAR-on-Y null by verify/p36_verify_p2_mnar_arm_mcse_2026-10-07.py: listwise 0.00181 ± 0.00009 against the 0.00183 the formula predicts, pooled 0.00146 ± 0.00007 against 0.00141, group-wise 0.00218 ± 0.00011 against neither candidate.

text.text: The group-wise column is quoted to coarser precision on purpose: its yardstick is measured rather than derived, so a multiple of -16 carries about ±0.8 of its own.
All three yardsticks are measured under mechanism 1 and applied across all four rows.

Selection on X leaves the within-group pair non-normal, so for rows 2 to 4 each is an approximation; a 10% error there would move -22.5 to between -20 and -25 and changes nothing a reader takes from the table.
The exact-zero boundary is specific to selection on Y (Figure 4).

text.text: Under group-asymmetric MNAR on X it fails: a difference appears where none exists.
Symmetric MNAR is harmless -both groups distort identically and the difference cancels -so it is the asymmetry in an X-dependent mechanism that breaks it, exactly as the proof's structure predicts.
But the practical rule survives, and for an instructive reason.
The distortion is not produced by the imputation.

Listwise deletion is the most displaced arm (-22.5 SE): selection on X restricts X's range in group 1, attenuating that group's correlation, so the estimand is compromised before any imputation happens.
Group-wise imputation, fitted to those same selected cases, carries a displaced limit of its own (-16 SE)close to listwise's and not equal to it.

The two probability limits are -0.0429 and -0.0369, computed exactly by quadrature over the selection law (verify/p36_verify_p2_mnar_plims_2026-10-07.py), so neither arm reproduces one common compromised quantity.
That 0.0060 gap is exact rather than estimated, which is why the single realisations in the table -each within about one standard error of its own limit -could not have settled it.
Pooled imputation is the least displaced (-14.1 SE) -because it does what it always does, shrink the two groups toward each other, which here shrinks a spurious difference toward zero.

Finite-sample Type I error at N = 320 (R = 1000) confirms the practical consequence, and it inverts the usual ordering: under the worst mechanism the pooled arm rejects at 0.004 while group-wise imputation reaches 0.073 -2.8 MCSE above nominal.

The congenial arm is the anti-conservative one here because of its own displacement rather than because congeniality reproduces a compromised target: group-wise imputation fitted to X-selected cases has a displaced limit of its own, and that displacement is large against its intervals.
Pooled imputation remains ultra-conservative, because its displacement is small relative to its intervals.
This is not an argument for pooling.
It is a reminder that under MNAR on X the damage is done before any imputation runs.

None of the three procedures tested here models X-dependent selection, so none of them could repair it; a repair would need a selection model this design does not identify, and these four mechanisms neither supply one nor rule one out.

The reading rule survives this stress test, with its scope stated precisely: where the groups share both a slope and a residual variance, pooled imputation did not inflate a group difference relative to a congenial analysis of the same data under any of the four mechanisms tested here -MAR on Y, symmetric MNAR on X, group-asymmetric MNAR on X, and opposed MNAR on X. Under MAR on Y that is a proved statement: the closed form cannot move the null at all.
Under MNAR on X it is a numerical finding on four mechanisms, not a theorem: it moves, but less than the alternatives do, and we have no derivation covering arbitrary selection functions.
The shared-slope antecedent is not decoration.

Drop it and the rule fails outright: with equal correlations and a two-fold difference in the spread of Y, the pooled plim is -0.1210 while the congenial arm sits at -1.1 × 10⁻¹⁶ (results/sequel_manufacture_scale.csv).
That is pooled imputation inflating a difference relative to a congenial analysis of the same data, which is exactly what the unqualified rule forbids. §4b is that case.
4b. …but it can manufacture one when the groups differ in scale Source: R/drv004_general.R, R/verify_drv004_general.R.
The general form ( §Theory, "The general form") shows the boundary needs the groups to share the slope β_g = ρ_g•σ_Xg/σ_Yg and the residual variance τ²_g = σ²_Xg(1 -ρ²_g) -not the correlation.
In the standardised design all three are the same condition, which is how we came to state it as a claim about correlations.
They are not the same in general.

Take ρ₁ = ρ₂ = 0.40 exactly -no true difference -with σ_X = 1 in both groups, MAR on Y at 40% calibrated within each group so the rates match, and let the groups differ only in the spread of Y. Matching the rates does not match the strength: the selection model acts on the raw outcome, so the group with the wider Y is selected at a higher effective standardised strength, and the contrast below carries that alongside the scale difference.
Varying σ_X instead is much weaker and not even monotone in sign (+0.0021 at a two-fold ratio, -0.0387 at four-fold), because it moves β_g and τ²_g together and the two effects partly cancel.
Scale heterogeneity in the incomplete variable is therefore the mild case; heterogeneity in Y -the variable selection acts onmanufactures the difference.
Every case above moves the slope and the residual variance together, so none of them shows that the second condition does any work on its own.
Scaling σ_X and σ_Y by the same factor holds β_g exactly fixed while τ²_g = σ²_Xg(1 -ρ²_g) grows with it.

The completed covariance then comes out exactly right -b equals each group's own slope -and the entire distortion arrives through Var_g(X*): σ_Y ratio plim N = 80 N = 160 N = 320 N = 640 1 (control) 0 0.000 0.002 0.002 0.001 1.5 -0.074 0.002 0.006 0.017 0.033 2 -0.121 0.007 0.019 0.035 0.149 3 -0.173 0.026 0.056 0.124 0.309 (rejection rate of the false null; nominal 0.05.
At π = 0.20 the same pattern is milder: 0.017 → 0.133 for ratio 3.)
Type I error rises with sample size in every configuration with unequal spread, and across those six configurations it grows from N = 80 to N = 640 by factors of 2.3 to 21.
The two ratio-1 controls do not rise, which is what makes them controls: at π = 0.20 the rate ends at 0.013 against a starting 0.014, and at π = 0.40 it stays within 0.002 of zero throughout.
So the growth is a scale effect and not something sample size does on its own.
At N = 640 with 40% missing and a three-fold standard-deviation ratio -a nine-fold variance ratio -31% of analyses declare a correlation difference that does not exist, six times the nominal rate.
Group-wise imputation holds 0.033-0.059 across the entire grid.
(One of the eighteen sample-size steps in those six configurations is non-monotone -ratio 2, π = .20, between N = 160 and N = 320 -a drop of 0.008 against a combined MCSE of 0.007, i.e.
Monte Carlo noise, reported rather than smoothed.
Over the full grid of eight configurations, the two controls included, four of twenty-four steps fall: three inside the controls, where no rise is expected, and that one.)
The manufactured difference is the coverage collapse again, pointing the other way
The mechanism is the one from §2 and the arithmetic is identical.
The manufactured ζ is fixed in N while its standard error falls like 1/√N, so the ratio of the two grows without bound and the false null is rejected more and more often.
Under the alternative that process destroys coverage; under the null it destroys Type I control.
Both are the same fixed-bias-with-shrinking-interval structure, and both get worse with exactly the thing researchers use to make results more trustworthy.
The practical consequence is sharper than the attenuation result.
A small study in these designs will usually not detect the artefact; a large one will report it as a significant finding.

As N → ∞ the rejection rate goes to 1 whenever the pooled procedure's limiting contrast is a fixed nonzero number, because that defect stays put while the interval shrinks like 1/√N. The asymptotic claim therefore needs a nonzero limiting contrast, and unequal group variances are not sufficient for one.
Heterogeneity in Y, the variable selection acts on, delivers it here: a two-fold ratio in σ_Y manufactures -0.1210 against the +0.0021 a two-fold ratio in σ_X manufactures ( §4b above).
And two groups with no association at all keep the contrast at exactly zero, at every rate and at any spread ratio, because both then share the slope zero ( §Appendix).
That is an asymptotic statement about the rejection probability, not a guarantee about any one finite sample.
Sources: results/sequel_applied_iris.csv (R = 2000), results/sequel_applied_plim.csv; figure results/sequel_applied.png.

In base-R iris, sepal length and sepal width are positively associated within each species, and the strength differs: r = 0.743 in setosa and 0.457 in virginica (N = 100, 50 per species), so the complete-data Fisher-z contrast is ζ_full = z(0.743) -z(0.457) = 0.4623, SE 0.2063, z = 2.24, p = 0.025almost exactly the simulated design value, and significant.
An analyst with complete data reports the species difference.
We treat that as the benchmark, impose MAR missingness on sepal width (logit P = a + 0.7•z(sepal length)) 2000 times, and re-estimate.
Figure 7 shows the result on data every reader of this journal has loaded: a species difference significant on complete data, and gone after the default imputation.

Group-wise imputation detects it as often as listwise deletion does.
The pooled model does not merely cost power; it removes the effect. 5a.

The real data transports the theory to a design it was not derived for This is a worked application on one familiar dataset, repeatedly masked -a transport check, not replication across datasets or data-generating processes.
The population the quadrature evaluates is a bivariate normal fitted to iris, so every "exact" figure below is exact in that fitted population and not in the finite, non-normal sample.
The applied κ of 0.850 at π = 0.40 is far above the balanced design's closed-form 0.4567, and the reason is that iris carries both of this paper's mechanisms at once.
The two species differ in correlation, which §3 shows pooled imputation shrinks.

They also differ in the spread of sepal length -within-species standard deviations of 0.373 and 0.673 in the shared standardised units, a 1.80-fold ratio -which is §4b's condition for pooled imputation to manufacture a difference where none exists.
Both act in the same direction, and §5b below shows that on this dataset they add.
The selection is also asymmetric: virginica has longer sepals, so the same missingness rule strips 53% of its values against setosa's 27%.
That asymmetry is real, and on its own it accounts for almost none of the excess -the control in §5b holds it in full and removes it anyway.

R/applied_plim_exact.R evaluates the identical procedure by quadrature -generalising the closed form to unequal group means, SDs and missingness rates, which the symmetric version does not cover -giving the plim exactly: π plim κ, pooled plim κ, group-wise 0.20 0.3381 -4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ 0.40 0.7001 -1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵
Two things there are worth pausing on.

The group-wise plim is exactly zero to machine precision although selection is strongly asymmetric -in the fitted normal population, group-wise imputation is not approximately unbiased for this estimand but exactly unbiased, which no simulation can establish.
That is a property of the model-based mechanism check, not of the iris sample itself: complication (i) below reports the offset the real, non-normal data carry on top of it.
And the pooled slope the imputation model targets is 0.890 at π = .20 and 0.953 at π = .40, nowhere near the symmetric-design value (ρ₁+ρ₂)/2 = 0.600.
Two effects separate them, and the larger one has nothing to do with missing data.

The pooled model X ~Y + species estimates a variance-weighted average of the two within-species slopes -1.81 and 0.52 in the shared standardised units -and that average already sits at 0.826 on the complete data.

Selection on Y then supplies the rest: it strips more of virginica, whose sepals are the longer ones, so the species that keeps more rows weighs more heavily in the fit and the slope rises from 0.826 to 0.953.
At π = .40 the complete-data gap accounts for 64% of the distance from 0.600 and selection for 36%; at π = .20 the split is 78% and 22% (verify/p36_n7_iris_pooled_slope_2026-10-07.py).

So §Theory's asymmetric-selection caveat applies on top of a comparator that was never right for this dataset: a slope stops matching a correlation as soon as the groups' spreads differ, and here they differ 1.80-fold.
A simulated plim (R/verify_applied_plim.R) agrees to 0.0017 and 0.0013, which is its proper role -a check on the exact computation, not the source of the number.
Listwise deletion, not covered by the quadrature module, has a simulated plim κ of -0.013/-0.013.
(i) Every arm at N = 100 sits above its plim by a common amount (+0.08 at π = .20, +0.15 at π = .40)including the two arms whose plim is ≈ 0, so it cannot be an imputation effect.

An MCAR control on the real sample, deleting at the same per-species rates but completely at random, returns κ = +0.003 and -0.011, against +0.065 and +0.133 for that same listwise arm under the mechanism -a twentieth and an eighth of the size.
The offset is therefore MAR range restriction acting on the actual iris points, which the fitted normal population understates because real sepal measurements are not exactly bivariate normal.
The offset is a property of the data and affects every method alike.

(ii) The closed form therefore describes the incremental attenuation that pooling adds on top of group-wise imputation -and that agrees with the plim almost exactly: π plim (pooled -group-wise), exact observed at N = 100 difference 0.20 0.3381 0.3442 +0.0061 0.40 0.7001 0.6902 -0.0099
A closed form derived for a balanced, exactly bivariate-normal design predicts the damage done on an unbalanced, not-quite-normal real dataset to within 0.010.

That agreement is worth having, but it cannot by itself identify which mechanism did the damage: both sides of it -the quadrature and the simulationare computed on the same design, carrying the same unequal means, unequal spreads and unequal deletion rates, so a comparison between them cannot separate §3's shrinkage from §4b's manufactured difference.
The check that can separate them is in §5b.
A second dataset, or a held-out design, would still be needed before calling any of this empirical generality, and we do not.

A plim estimated by simulation gives 0.0005 and 0.0059 here, which is too flattering: the simulated plim itself moves by 0.004 between N = 10⁶ and N = 2 × 10⁶, so its own Monte Carlo noise is the size of the agreement it is being used to demonstrate.
The quadrature values carry no such noise and the honest figure is 0.010.
The residual gap is now interpretable rather than ambiguous: it is the real data's departure from the fitted normal model, the same departure that produces the common offset in (i).

The two mechanisms add, on this dataset §5a leaves one question open: the paper proves two separate failures, and iris satisfies the conditions for both, so how much of the applied damage belongs to each?

Write displacement for how far the pooled estimate falls below the truth -ζ_full minus the probability limit of ζ , so §5a's κ times 0.4623 -and compare three designs, each simulated from the procedure at N = 2 × 10⁶ per replication, 36 replications (verify/p36_verify_p2_applied_decomposition_2026-10-06.py, written from the method and sharing no code with R/applied_plim_exact.R): • A, the real design -the iris fit exactly as above.
• B, the balanced design -the same two correlations, both species standard normal with equal means.
This is the design §Theory derives its closed form for, so B is §3's mechanism acting alone.
• C, the null design -the iris fit with the two correlations set equal to their mean, so the true contrast is zero and any displacement that appears is manufactured.

§Results 2 reports that nominal 95% coverage of ζ falls from 0.992 at N = 40 to 0.703 at N = 320, and the Discussion explains it as a fixed bias divided by a shrinking interval.

That explanation is a theorem, stated with its hypotheses in the companion paper on the interaction (Paper 1, Appendix §G, Result G1): if the estimate converges in probability to a constant T*, the reported half-width converges in probability to a constant h*, and the asymptotic defect Δ = |T* -T| against the target T satisfies h* < Δ, then coverage tends to zero.
text.formatted: That explanation is a theorem, stated with its hypotheses in the companion paper on the interaction (Paper 1, Appendix §G, Result G1): if the estimate converges in probability to a constant T*, the reported half-width converges in probability to a constant h*, and the asymptotic defect Δ = |T* -T| against the target T satisfies h* < Δ, then coverage tends to zero.

text.text: The proof is three lines and turns on nothing more than the reverse triangle inequality and a union bound.
The strict inequality is necessary, and that is why we quote all three cases.

Result G1 is a trichotomy in the comparison between the settled half-width h* and the asymptotic defect Δ: (a) h* < Δ sends coverage to zero; (b) h* > Δ sends it to one; (c) h* = Δ determines nothing, and every value in [0, 1] is attainable as the limit.
text.formatted: Result G1 is a trichotomy in the comparison between the settled half-width h* and the asymptotic defect Δ: (a) h* < Δ sends coverage to zero; (b) h* > Δ sends it to one; (c) h* = Δ determines nothing, and every value in [0, 1] is attainable as the limit.

text.text: So a fixed, non-vanishing defect does not by itself destroy coverage.
Case (b) is the counterexample: hold Δ fixed, let the reported interval settle at a width above it, and coverage goes to one rather than to zero.

Case (a) therefore needs both halves -a defect that does not vanish and a width that settles strictly below it -and the word strictly carries weight, because at the boundary h* = Δ a width approaching Δ from below drives coverage to zero while one approaching from above drives it to one.
Quoting only case (a) would leave a reader with the much stronger and false reading that bias alone is enough.
This paper's estimand is an instance of Result G1.
Take T = ζ, the true Fisher-z contrast, and T_n = ζ the pooled-imputation estimate.
Step 6 gives plim which at π = 0.40 and ρ = (.6, .2) is 0.4567 ×0.490 = 0.224 -a fixed number, not something that shrinks with the sample.

The reported interval is built by Rubin's rules on the Fisher-z scale, and its half-width goes to zero in probability because the m completed-data estimates share a probability limit, the within-imputation variance 1/(n₁ -3) + 1/(n₂ -3) vanishes deterministically, and the Barnard-Rubin multiplier is bounded in probability rather than convergent to a constant (Paper 1, §G, Result G2).

Boundedness is all Result G2 asks of it, and the multiplier stays random in the limit because the fraction of missing information does: with m fixed at 20, the multiplier's fifth to ninety-fifth percentiles hold at 1.965 to 1.982 from n = 160 to n = 20480 rather than narrowing (verify/p36_n1_p2_multiplier_2026-10-07.py).
So h* = 0 < Δ and coverage tends to zero.

text.text: ∎ Three qualifications matter for how §Results 2 should be read.

The defect must be written as a difference, not as a ratio, at the true null. κ(π) is defined as (ζ -plim ζ )/ζ and is undefined when ζ = 0, which is exactly the manufactured-contrast case of §Results 4b; there Δ = |plim ζ -0| is a manufactured nonzero number and the corollary still applies, but only in the difference form.

The conclusion is a limit, not a direction at every N. Coverage tending to zero does not imply that it falls at every sample size, and the grid in §Results 2 should be described as showing when the collapse arrives rather than as evidence of monotone decay.
And κ(π) = 0 is not a safe harbour.
Where the groups share slope and residual variance the defect vanishes and this corollary says nothing -in either direction.
A separate argument, not this one, is what would establish that coverage is then correct.
Everything above assumes the design of the simulation: equal groups, Y standard normal in both, identical selection.
Real data satisfy none of that.

The Appendix drops all three and restates the boundary in the form the algebra actually supportsif the groups share both the slope β_g and the residual variance τ²_g, then a zero contrast stays zero: ζ = 0 ⟹ plim ζ = 0, for any selection on Y.

Those two conditions are sufficient, and -once the missing rate varies -necessary: for two groups the contrast survives at every rate only when the slope is shared and the residual variance is too, with the one trivial exception that neither group has any association at all.
That holds for any positive group shares and any positive outcome variances, equal or not (Appendix).

The Appendix also records the object underneath both statements: under missingness completely at random the pooled moments are straight lines in the missing rate, so the bias is the imputed rows' failure to satisfy the analysis's own normal equations.
That failure being zero is normal-equation compatibility, which is weaker than congeniality in Meng's (1994) sense.
A correlation is a ratio of those moments rather than a coefficient in them, which is why this paper's estimand needs the further step the Appendix takes by hand.
The special case makes the two look like one, which is how we came to state the boundary as a claim about equal correlations; §Results 4b reports what happens when they come apart.

Where it is used What happens without it Missingness depends on Y only Step 1 E[X|Y,R=1] ≠ ρ_g•Y, so the observed part no longer carries ρ_g cleanly and the complete-case slope becomes biased as well.

Selection on Y already biases the complete-case correlation: it shrinks Var(Y | R=1) to 0.907 at 40% missing and range-restricts each group's correlation with it, which displaces the contrast by -0.019 ( §Results 1) Within-group bivariate normality Steps 1, 5 the conditional mean may be non-linear; the pooled-slope mechanism survives, the closed form does not Equal groups, common Y distribution, symmetric selection Steps 3-6 of the special case only superseded by §"The general form", which drops all of it: b becomes a variance-weighted average of the within-group slopes and the identity becomes 𝒜_g + ℬ_g = σ²_Yg Var(Y) = 1 Step 6 rescaling only; correlations are scale-invariant Nothing in the mechanism requires the missingness rate to be equal across groups, and nothing requires the two correlations to have the same sign -the (0.5, -0.1) design is verified at step level too.
If the analysis lets groups differ, the imputation model must let them differ in the same way.

When the estimand is a between-group difference in association, this means imputing within group -or using an imputation model that gives each group its own conditional slope and its own residual variance.
Adding group as a main effect is not a partial fix but no fix at all, because it leaves the entire attenuation in place: what is pooled is the slope, not the means.

Adding the group × predictor interaction to one homoscedastic regression is a partial fix and not an equivalent one, which is worth saying because it is the easier thing to do in standard software: it frees the slopes and still pools the residual variance, so the completed variance stays wrong whenever the groups' residual variances differ, and that is one of the two mechanisms this paper reports.

At β = (0.8, 1.3), τ² = (0.5, 1.4) and outcome variances 1 and 4, the interaction-only model misses a group's correlation by up to 0.111, while the same model with equal residual variances is exact (verify/p36_verify_p2_exact_recovery_2026-10-02.
The cost of doing so is small.
Across the whole grid, group-wise imputation held bias within [-0.016, +0.021] and coverage within [0.936, 0.974], so it purchased its accuracy at no measurable price in efficiency.
In the applied illustration it detected the real species difference as often as listwise deletion did.
We therefore see no efficiency argument for pooling in this setting.
Because the failure is one-directional under a statable condition, the reading rule is asymmetric, and the asymmetry is the practically useful part.
A study that used default imputation and reported no difference is uninformative about whether one exists.
At 40% missing, the procedure removes roughly half the difference on the z scale, and in the applied case it removed all of the detections.
That a null report is uninformative holds whatever the groups look like.

The attenuation itself, however, is one-directional only within the class we model -standardised groups, a common Y distribution, selection on Y. Outside it the general form permits the completed contrast to be shrunk, exaggerated, reversed or manufactured, which leaves a null report uninformative for a wider set of reasons rather than for this one.
A study that used default imputation and did report a difference cannot be cleared by inspecting its variances.

The "erase only" reading holds only when the null case has a common population conditional slope and residual variance, and comparable-looking marginal sample variances do not establish that: two groups with equal correlations and unequal spread already have unequal slopes, and sampling error puts the required equality beyond the reach of any eyeball check.
The defensible rule is procedural rather than diagnostic:

A pooled-imputation result should be re-estimated with group-specific slopes and residual distributions, or under an explicitly congenial joint model, before the reported difference is treated as established.
Comparable observed variances are at most a weak warning diagnostic, never a guarantee.

Where the groups' variances visibly differ, the finding warrants reanalysis with group-specific conditional models rather than outright rejection, and a large study reports the artefact as significant more often than a small one does.

With equal true correlations and a two-fold difference in the spread of the complete variable, pooled imputation manufactures ζ = -0.121 out of nothing; at a three-fold ratio with 40% missing and N = 640 it declares that difference significant in 31% of analyses ( §Results 4b).
The rejection rate rises with N and tends to 1 in those designs, because each has a fixed nonzero contrast limit.
Unequal variances alone do not produce one: two groups with no association at all keep a zero contrast exactly, at every rate and at any spread ratio ( §Appendix).
The asymmetry we originally claimed, that pooling can erase but never manufacture, is real in the standardised design and not beyond it.

Its engine is that a true null there forces a common X | Y slope and a common residual variance, which is the class pooling leaves untouched, while a real difference forces unequal slopes and is shrunk.

Equal correlations with unequal scales breaks the first condition; equal correlations and equal slopes with unequal spread breaks the second; and either breach alone puts the null outside the untouched class and makes the failure run in both directions.
We state the condition prominently because the weaker, unconditional version is the more quotable one, and because it is wrong.
That rule differs from the one governing the companion paper's deterministic regression imputation, which can manufacture an effect under much broader conditions.
Keeping the two straight matters, because the summary "uncongenial imputation is dangerous" is too coarse to act on.
The kind of danger depends on which member of the family the analyst used.
The coverage result is neither a paradox nor new asymptotics.
It is the standard consequence of an inconsistent estimator combined with a shrinking interval, for which Morris, White and Crowther (2019, p. 2087) give the general statement.
text.formatted: It is the standard consequence of an inconsistent estimator combined with a shrinking interval, for which Morris, <ref type="bibr">White and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Crowther (2019, p. 2087)</ref> give the general statement.

text.text: Since the bias is proportional to the estimand and roughly constant in N, while the standard error falls at rate 1/√N, the ratio of the two grows without bound, and the interval becomes both narrower and no better centred.
In our grid, coverage at π = 0.40 runs 0.992, 0.974, 0.903 and 0.703 as N goes from 40 to 320, reaching 0.584 on the robustness design.
The practical trap lies in the direction of the error at small N. The pooled arm looks better than nominal when the sample is small, because between-imputation variance inflates its intervals.
A researcher piloting at N = 40 therefore sees conservative intervals, concludes that the method is safe, and scales up into precisely the regime where it fails.
The same structure produces the false positives reported in §Results 4b, and the two are best understood as one phenomenon rather than as two findings.

Applied to a real difference, that growing ratio destroys coverage; applied to a manufactured one, it destroys Type I control, which rises from 0.026 to 0.309 as N goes from 80 to 640 in the worst cell.
Every diagnostic a researcher might use for reassurance, whether more data, tighter intervals, or a significant result, moves in the wrong direction.
The two papers describe the same mechanism with different consequences.

In both, an imputation model omits a term that the analysis model contains, and the estimand attached to that term is attenuated by approximately the missing fraction, with an exact factor κ(π) -not the same κ.
At the 40% both papers headline, ours is 0.457 and the companion's 0.384, either side of 0.400.
The companion's factor crosses below π near 0.32; ours never does in our range.
The companion's omitted term is a product X₁X₂, whereas this paper's is group × Y.

Figure 8 puts both papers' attenuation factors on one pair of axes -ours, and the companion's under both MAR and MCAR, three curves in all -which is legitimate because each κ is the same kind of quantity: the dimensionless fraction of a true effect destroyed.
They are not the same curve.
Against the companion's MAR factor, ours agrees to 0.010 for π ≤ 0.10 and separates to 0.087 by π = 0.50, with pooling across groups costing more than omitting an interaction at every rate.
Both factors are evaluated by quadrature, so the small-π agreement is a feature of the curves, not a limit on the comparison.
The instructive difference lies in the boundary, and it is narrower than the symmetry suggests.

Deterministic regression imputation manufactures interactions that are not there, governed in sign by a single selection moment though not in magnitude, and it does so under a wide range of conditions.

Pooled imputation is guaranteed not to manufacture a correlation difference whenever the groups match on both the slope and the residual variance, since the closed form then returns exactly zero for any selection on Y; the designs in which we have seen it manufacture one are designs where the groups differ in scale.

The two failures are therefore not opposites: one is broadly prone to false positives, the other conditionally so -and its condition concerns population slopes and residual variances, so unequal observed group variances flag the risk rather than measuring it.
One selection mechanism.
Everything reported here assumes missingness at random on the fully observed variable Y, with a logistic tilt of fixed strength.
That assumption is what makes E[X | Y, observed] = ρ_g•Y hold, and hence what makes the closed form clean.

It also means that the specific shape of κ(π), in particular the finding that κ/π declines from 1.40 to 1.07 across π, is a property of this mechanism rather than a universal constant of pooled imputation.
Missingness depending on X itself is now partly covered rather than merely disclaimed ( §Results 4a).
The exact-zero boundary turns out to be specific to selection on Y: under group-asymmetric MNAR on X, a difference does appear under the null.

The practical rule nevertheless survives, because the distortion originates in the mechanism rather than in the imputation, with listwise deletion the most displaced arm and pooled imputation the least.
In that setting the pooled arm's Type I error is 0.004, while the congenial group-wise arm reaches 0.073, which is 2.8 Monte Carlo standard errors above nominal.

The congenial arm is the anti-conservative one there because of its own displacement rather than because congeniality reproduces a compromised target: group-wise imputation fitted to X-selected cases has a displaced limit of its own, -0.0369 against listwise's -0.0429.
None of the three procedures models X-dependent selection, so the experiment does not show that no imputation model could.
We have not covered MNAR combined with genuinely different correlations, or missingness driven by an unobserved third variable.
κ depends on the gap, not only on π. κ is not a function of π alone.

It rises with |ρ₁ -ρ₂|, from 0.448 at a gap of 0.10 to 0.539 at a gap of 0.90 with π = 0.40, although it is very nearly unaffected by where the two correlations sit, since two pairs sharing a gap at different levels agree to 0.001.
That near-invariance is a numerical finding over the levels we evaluated; we have no proof of exact invariance, and the phrase should not be read as one.
For the gaps most studies test, meaning 0.4 or less, the variation is under 0.01 and κ(π) may be read as a one-argument function, but the qualification belongs in any statement of the law.
That variation is inside the ±0.01 noise floor of a Monte Carlo evaluator, which is how it reads as invariance; at a gap of 0.90 it is eight times that floor.
An invariance claim needs an evaluator finer than the effect it is testing.
Normality.
Within-group bivariate normality is assumed and used twice.

The applied illustration is reassuring rather than decisive, since real sepal measurements are not exactly normal and the incremental prediction survived to 0.010 -its worst discrepancy across the two rates, +0.0061 at π = .20 and -0.0099 at π = .40 -but that is a single dataset.
