The covariance is exactly right.
The variance is not, unless τ²_g = τ² as well.
So the boundary needs two things, and the special case hid the second by making them the same condition: Sufficient -and necessary, once the missing rate is allowed to vary.

Both completed moments are affine in the observed fraction, so matching the groups at every rate is a set of coefficient equations, not the one scalar equation that made cancellation look unavoidable.
Solved, they force both conditions: a shared slope alone leaves the variance wrong, a shared residual variance alone the covariance.
Cancellation at a single rate survives, and the recorded example does it at 3/5 and nowhere else.
Say what "every rate" buys, because the quantifier carries the whole claim and costs nothing to state.

For two groups under missingness completely at random at a fraction common to both, with any positive group shares and any positive outcome variances -equal or not -the completed Fisher-z contrast equals the true contrast at every observed fraction if and only if the groups share the slope, and share the residual variance unless that shared slope is zero.
The zero-slope case is the trivial exception: with no association in either group both completed correlations are zero at every rate whatever the residual variances are.

Necessity is proved here on the completely-at-random sub-family, which is the stronger reading rather than a weaker one -fewer mechanisms are needed to pin the two conditions down, and sufficiency above still holds for any selection on Y and any number of groups.

The same proof gives something sharper than the contrast statement, and it is the version worth carrying: under either admitted case each group's completed correlation is individually constant in the rate and equal to its true value.
The contrast is not preserved by two errors cancelling.

So pooled imputation cannot trade one group's distortion against the other's across a range of rates -it can do so at isolated rates, which is exactly what the 3/5 example is, and nothing in a real study tunes the missing rate to a point.
One limitation, and it is about detectability rather than about the algebra.

Necessity here is exact equality, and a search over the parameter space finds designs that break both conditions and still preserve the contrast to within 6 × 10⁻⁷ at every rate -a violation no finite sample could resolve.

So the boundary separates designs cleanly in the limit and not at all in practice near its edge, and a reanalysis that finds a stable contrast across missing rates has evidence the conditions nearly hold, not proof that they do.
The proof itself is symbolic: verify/p36_verify_p2_unequal_variance_necessity_2026-09-16.wls solves the coefficient equations and admits only the two cases above.

R/verify_p2_uniform_necessity.R carries the zero-slope exception and the detectability search, and it is numerical evidence that fails to contradict the proof rather than the proof -its own verdict line says so.
Both are deposited.
Under the standardised design, ρ₁ = ρ₂ implies β₁ = β₂ and τ²₁ = τ²₂, which is why the boundary looked like a statement about equal correlations.
It is not.

Equal correlations with unequal scales give unequal slopes, and then pooled imputation manufactures a difference -see §Results 4b, where ρ₁ = ρ₂ = 0.40 and a two-fold difference in σ_Y produces a plim of ζ = -0.121.
The general form above drops all three of the body's symmetries -equal groups, Y standard normal in both, identical selection.

The identity becomes 𝒜_g + ℬ_g = Var(Y | g), the pooled slope becomes a variance-weighted average of the within-group slopes, and the boundary is restated in the form the algebra supportsa shared slope β_g and a shared residual variance τ²_g are together sufficient for a zero contrast to stay zero, for any selection on Y -and, in the rate, necessary.

That correction matters in the body, not only in the appendix: the special case makes those two conditions look like one, which is how we came to state the boundary as a claim about equal correlations.
§Results 4b reports what happens when they come apart.
The general form is verified against simulation on three designs that break every symmetry -45 checks, 0 failures (R/verify_drv004_general.R).
The closed form is evaluated by quadrature, not by Monte Carlo.

Every moment in the derivation ( §Theory) is a one-dimensional integral of a normal density against a logistic weight; estimating them by simulation at N = 4 × 10⁶ leaves roughly ±0.01 of noise on κ, which is the same size as some of the effects below and would make them undetectable. zeta_plim_exact() in R/drv004_closedform.R integrates them directly and reproduces all four independently verified designs.

κ moves with the gap between the correlations, not with their level κ is nearly invariant to the level, but not to the gap. κ depends on π alone to within 0.010 across three designs, which is inside the noise floor of the Monte Carlo evaluator.

Evaluated exactly by quadrature, κ moves with the gap between the two correlations and is nearly invariant to their level: the five designs, and the two sharing a gap of 0.40 at different levels that agree to within 0.001, are tabulated in §Results.

Three things follow from having the closed form that the simulation alone would not give: 2. κ can be read off before collecting data, for any π, from quadrature rather than a new simulation -which is what makes the result usable as a planning quantity.
It says which feature of the design controls the damage.
The attenuation runs through A_g, the observed-case share within each group.

We offered that as a prediction rather than a post-hoc account, and §Results 5b has since tested it and rejected it: holding the asymmetric deletion rates almost fixed at 0.267 / 0.532 while equalising the two species' spreads and correlations drops the manufactured displacement from 0.1227 to 0.0001.
So the uneven loss of values accounts for essentially none of the applied illustration's excess over the balanced simulation, and the 1.80-fold spread ratio supplies it instead.
Restated here, not cited, so this appendix stands on its own.

text.text: Everything above computes completed moments and then forms a correlation from them.
It is worth recording what governs those moments, because the same three lines govern every estimand of this kind -and because they say precisely where this paper's estimand is different.
Write an analysis as a regression of an outcome on a feature vector Z, and let G = E[ZZ′] and c = E[ZY] be its population moments, so the true coefficients are β = G⁻¹c.

Under missingness completely at random at rate π, a fraction 1π of rows carry the real features and a fraction π carry features built from an imputed value, so G*(π) = (1π)G + πG_imp, c*(π) = (1π)c + πc_imp, and neither imputed-row moment set depends on π.
Both pooled moments are straight lines in the missing rate.

The bias is then exactly β*β = G*(π)⁻¹(c*(π) -G*(π)β), and differentiating at π = 0 gives the first-order cost as -G⁻¹d, where is the moment defect of the imputed rows: how far the filled-in rows fall from satisfying the analysis's own normal equations.
The estimator is exact at every missing rate exactly when d = 0.

That is normalequation compatibility, not a definition of congeniality in Meng's (1994) sense, which is stronger: preserving the whole imputation/substantive-model relationship forces d = 0, while d = 0 can also arise through cancellation without it.
The condition d = 0 is nonetheless sharper than asking the imputation to preserve the joint distribution, which is sufficient for exactness but stronger than necessary.

With the Gram matrix held fixed, a regression coefficient is linear in the cross-moment vector, so the defect converts to a coefficient error in one matrix multiplication -by G*(π)⁻¹ exactly, and by G⁻¹ at first order in the rate.
Jointly in both moment sets the coefficient is not linear at all: G⁻¹c is scale-invariant, since multiplying G and c by one constant leaves it unchanged.
A correlation admits no such conversion.
It is a ratio, σ_XY ⁄ σ_X σ_Y, and the contrast then applies Fisher's transform on top.

So the law above does not deliver ζ directly; it delivers the moments, and the ratio and the transform are a further step -which is exactly the step Results 2 through 5 of this appendix take, by hand, for this design.
Two things follow that are worth stating plainly.
The moments this paper computes are the same objects the general law consumes, which is why the pooled slope b appears in both accounts as the thing the imputed rows are told to believe.

And the nonlinearity is not a technicality: because a correlation is a ratio, a defect in the covariance and a defect in the variance can partly cancel, which is precisely why the boundary condition above is necessary only once the missing rate is allowed to vary, and why a single rate can hide a real difference.
We see the broader contrast though some details stay concealed Pooling can erase a difference or make a false one seem revealed

That exact null is a proof that pooled imputation cannot manufacture a difference in this standardised design, where equal correlations give equal slopes and equal residual variances; a simulation could only ever fail to find one.The same algebra gives more than the null, and the general version is worth stating. k_g = 0 requires a shared conditional slope, and leaving the completed variance alone requires a shared residual variance; neither requirement needs ρ₁ = ρ₂ or equal outcome variances.

Then the pooled imputer recovers exactly those values, b = β and s² = τ², and the completed moments within group g are Cov_g(X, Y) = β•Var(Y | g) and Var_g(X ) = β²•Var(Y | g) + τ² -the group's own population moments, with the missing rate absent from both.

So each correlation is preserved exactly, and so is any contrast between them, zero or not, at every rate and under any admitted selection on Y. Unequal outcome variances are permitted and then the preserved contrast is nonzero: at β = 0.8, τ² = 0.5 and Var(Y | g) = 1 against 4, the true ζ = -0.584 comes back unchanged at every rate (closed form and simulation at N = 4 × 10⁶, with controls that fire when either equality is broken: verify/p36_verify_p2_exact_recovery_2026-10-02.

Within this class pooled imputation does not shrink a real difference either, so the asymmetry of §Discussion is a property of the standardised design -where a null forces the class and a real difference leaves itand not of the class itself.
